When an attendee or a team admin adds guests, updateCalendarAttendees runs with credentials that do not own the booking's calendar references. The update fails or throws, and because it is not caught, the request errors even though the attendee rows are already saved. Use the booking user's credentials (booking.user.credentials) instead.

Error message fallback never applies

The message is built with a template string that always produces a non-empty value, even when err.data is missing (e.g. 'undefined: ...'). As a result, the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never be used.

No restriction on cancelled or past bookings, and no limit on number of guests

The handler does not check booking status. Any attendee can add an unbounded list of guests to any booking they belong to, including cancelled ones. Each added guest triggers outbound email, so this can be abused to spam arbitrary addresses.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete condition not scoped to SMS method

The second branch of the OR in deleteMany (`retryCount > 1`) has no `method: SMS` filter. This SMS cron will delete any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP ones. If other code paths increment retryCount for those methods, the SMS cron will delete their reminders. The condition should be scoped with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Update in catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch block is not guarded. If it fails (for example, the reminder was deleted concurrently, or a DB error occurs), the exception propagates out of the loop. The remaining reminders are not processed and the handler returns an error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Constructor accepts loose public options type, losing compile-time validation

The constructor now takes `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional for every scope. Previously the discriminated union type required `teamId` when scope is "team". Callers can now pass `scope: "team"` without a `teamId` and the code still compiles. At runtime, safeParse then fails and the service silently returns `1=0`, so callers get empty results with no error to point at the bad call.

Integration test relies on denormalized view and dropped caching tests

The caching tests were deleted even though the caching logic is still in the service, so that behaviour is no longer covered. The PR author also admits the tests were never run. The new `$queryRaw` test assumes the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` view exposes exactly these columns. Because nothing was executed, the SQL fragments' compatibility with the view (column quoting, `ANY` with int arrays) has not been verified.

findMany removed without migrating callers

The public `findMany` method is replaced by `getBaseConditions`, which returns a raw SQL fragment. Any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany`, such as insights routers, will break. Each caller now has to hand-write a raw query, and the PR does not update any of them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateMany with empty data does not bump updatedAt

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is called with an empty data object. Prisma's `updateMany` with no fields to set does not reliably issue an update, so `@updatedAt` is not refreshed. The stated goal of touching `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is therefore not met, and the call costs an extra query on every cache refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only

`sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed (Linux), the empty string is treated as the script and the command fails, so the env file is never updated. The relative path `ENV_FILE` also means the script only works when run from a specific directory.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError

A missing or unauthorized credential throws a plain `Error`. tRPC reports this as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN, so a client-side access error is surfaced as a server failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale

The cache timestamp is formatted with `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` instead of the user's locale. The surrounding text is translated, but non-English users will still see a US-format date.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion doesn't invalidate connectedCalendars query

The deleteCache mutation's `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. It never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. As a result the dropdown keeps showing the old "Last updated" cache status until a manual refetch, which this page disables on window focus. The disconnect mutation does invalidate this query; deleteCache should do the same.

Cache status shown even when calendar-cache feature disabled

The handler instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` directly and queries the DB, bypassing the feature-flag mock used elsewhere. Stale cache rows can therefore be shown, and can be deleted from the UI, even when calendar-cache is disabled for the user.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async reminder deletions are not awaited, so try/catch never catches their errors

deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called inside forEach without await. The surrounding try/catch therefore never sees their failures. The same fire-and-forget pattern appears in handleCancelBooking and the trpc routers. In serverless environments these promises may be dropped when the response returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels at SendGrid but never deletes the DB reminder

With immediateDelete=true (used for rescheduled bookings), the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting or flagging the WorkflowReminder row. The row stays with scheduled=true and cancelled=null, so it is orphaned. On reschedule, the old booking's reminders remain attached to the old booking in the DB. Each immediate cancel also counts toward SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation limit, which is the failure this PR sets out to avoid.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancelled but never-scheduled reminders can still be sent

If a reminder has no referenceId yet (scheduled=false), deleteScheduledEmailReminder deletes it, which is fine. However, a reminder can be marked cancelled after this function runs but before the cron's unscheduled-reminders query. The unscheduled query does not filter out cancelled=true, so cancelled reminders can be scheduled and sent. The cancellation query also lacks a method: EMAIL filter.

Cancelled reminders whose time passed between cron runs are deleted without being cancelled

The cron first deletes every email reminder with scheduledDate <= now, and only afterwards looks up cancelled reminders due within the next hour. Suppose a booking is cancelled less than about 15 minutes before its reminder time, so the reminder was never picked up by the previous cron run. That reminder is deleted by the first query before the cancellation step reaches it. Its SendGrid batch is never cancelled, and the email goes out for the cancelled booking.

One SendGrid failure aborts the entire cancellation batch

The whole cancellation loop sits inside a single try block. If any client.request call throws, for example because of a null referenceId or a rate limit, the loop stops. The remaining cancellations are skipped and the deletes already queued are never awaited. Error handling should happen per reminder.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach pushes to apiDeletes after it is awaited

The recurring-cancel branch uses `forEach(async ...)` and awaits `getCalendar` before pushing into `apiDeletes`. Those pushes happen after the synchronous code has moved on, so `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` has already captured the array and misses them.

As a result, calendar deletions for recurring bookings are not awaited, and their errors become unhandled rejections. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
All app modules are still imported eagerly at module load

Each property is written as `import("./x")`, and that call runs as soon as the object literal is evaluated. So every app package is still loaded when `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, and nothing is lazy. The PR's goal of deferring app loading is not met.

It also adds a risk: if any app module throws during load, its promise rejects with no handler attached. That surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection at startup.

The entries should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call sites should invoke them.

forEach(async) in requestReschedule leaves deletions unawaited

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside each callback. The returned promises are discarded, so the calendar and video deletions are fire-and-forget.

Any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The mutation may also return before the events are actually deleted.

getCalendarCredentials now returns calendar as a Promise

`calendar` in each returned item is now a `Promise<Calendar|null>`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it.

Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` that reads `.calendar` directly will get a Promise. Because a Promise is always truthy, those callers will either break or wrongly treat a missing calendar as present.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working hours end check uses slot start instead of slot end

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, the same value as `start`. A slot that begins inside working hours but ends after them passes the check. The intended end-of-slot validation never happens. `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === always false

The check that a date override marks the whole day unavailable compares two freshly created Dayjs instances with `===`. This is reference equality, so it is never true. Overrides where start equals end (a day marked unavailable) are not caught by this branch. They only behave correctly by accident through the later isBefore/isSame checks. Compare with `.isSame()` or `.valueOf()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any single non-matching working-hours entry rejects the slot

`workingHours.find` returns true as soon as any entry covering that weekday does not contain the slot. Users commonly have several availability ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17). A slot at 14:00 falls outside the 9-12 entry, so it is wrongly rejected. The logic should reject a slot only when no working-hours entry contains it (use `some` and negate).

Date override day comparison uses incorrectly shifted time

`date.start` is already an absolute UTC instant, yet the code adds the negated organizer offset to it before formatting the day. The result is then compared with the UTC slot date. For organizers far from UTC, the shift moves the override onto the wrong UTC calendar day. The start and end bounds are shifted the same way, so slots are wrongly accepted or rejected. Overrides near midnight UTC may never match, or may match the adjacent day.

Override minutes wrap across midnight

The override start and end are converted to minutes using `hour()*60+minute()` after applying the offset. If the shifted time crosses midnight, the value wraps. A shifted end at 00:30 the next day becomes 30, which is less than the start, and the slot range is silently dropped. Overrides near day boundaries in the invitee timezone are therefore lost.

Timezone test doesn't exercise the fixed-host round-robin fix

The new test only re-queries a single-user event in another invitee timezone. The headline fix, that date overrides of fixed hosts apply in round-robin events, has no test. The organizer/override timezone mismatch case is also not covered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration metadata lacks sender

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes the key exists. Integrations created through the pipeline, or older ones created before sender was stored, have no sender key. This raises a 500 instead of rendering the error page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
OAuth redirect URL parameters not URL-encoded

The redirect_uri and state are interpolated into the authorize URL without urlencode. The redirect_uri contains ':' and '/' characters and may contain query characters, which can corrupt the request to GitHub. Use urlencode to build the query string.

User verification skipped when Integration does not yet exist

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the view returns next_step() before the github_authenticated_user check runs. An attacker can supply any installation_id that has no webhook-created row yet and complete the pipeline without proving they installed it. build_integration fetches installation info and creates the integration anyway. The sender check is only enforced when a webhook-created row already exists, so the protection is bypassable.

get_user_info failures not handled

get_user_info makes an HTTP call to GitHub. If GitHub returns an error or the call raises, the exception is not caught and the user sees a 500 instead of the friendly error page. safe_urlopen at line 423 is also outside the try block, so network errors there are unhandled too.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued default evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once, when the module is imported. Every AssignmentSource created afterwards gets the same stale timestamp instead of its own creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance records when it was actually queued.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
datetime in task kwargs is not JSON-serializable

`asdict()` keeps `queued` as a datetime object, and the result is passed as Celery task kwargs. With JSON serialization this either fails to serialize, or arrives at the worker as a string. If it arrives as a string, `from_dict` still accepts it, because the frozen dataclass does no type checking. If serialization fails, the outbound sync task cannot be enqueued at all. Serialize `queued` explicitly, for example as an ISO string, and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New assignment_source kwarg passed to all sync_assignee_outbound implementations

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` for every provider. The abstract signature accepts `**kwargs`, but concrete implementations (Jira, Jira Server, VSTS, GitHub, etc.) that don't declare `**kwargs` will raise TypeError on every outbound assignee sync. None of those implementations are updated in this PR.

assignment_source added to sync_status_outbound but never passed

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter, but no caller passes it. Status sync cycles are therefore not addressed, and the signature change is misleading to implementers.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with only `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler leaves several abstract members unimplemented: counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values and build_occurrence_and_event_data. Any call to `detector.detector_handler` for a metric_alert_fire detector will therefore raise TypeError when it tries to instantiate the abstract class. Before this change the handler was a concrete no-op.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test builds expected occurrences with wrong values, hiding mismatches

Several tests build the expected occurrence with value=6 even though the evaluated value is 10, 100 or 8. In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue the expected occurrence also uses group key 'val1' while the code evaluates 'group_key'. These tests only pass because the mock ignores both the value and, effectively, the fingerprint in a way that coincidentally matches. As a result the assertions do not verify that the correct value and group key are passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
PriorityLevel(new_status) fails for detector levels with no PriorityLevel equivalent

The code converts a DetectorPriorityLevel to PriorityLevel by value. If DetectorPriorityLevel defines any non-OK value that PriorityLevel does not have, this raises ValueError and aborts evaluation for the whole packet. The surrounding state updates have already been enqueued at that point, so the enqueued state is left inconsistent with what was actually processed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed symbols may break existing imports and test mocks

`get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `mark_failed_threshold` and `SimpleCheckIn` were removed from `mark_failed.py` and moved elsewhere. `create_issue_platform_occurrence` was also renamed to `create_incident_occurrence`. No compatibility re-exports were left behind, and no test files were updated in this PR. Existing tests that patch `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.produce_occurrence_to_kafka` will stop intercepting the call, because the import now happens in `incident_occurrence.py`. Tests or other modules that import these names from `mark_failed` will fail with ImportError.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key 'shards' vs 'shard'

The `wait_produce` timer uses the tag key `shards`, while the neighbouring metrics use `shard`. This inconsistency breaks dashboards and queries that group by the shard tag.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process misses SpawnProcess

The processes are created through `get_context('spawn').Process`, so they are `SpawnProcess` instances. That class derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process`. The checks `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` are therefore always False. As a result, hung processes are never killed before a replacement is spawned, and join never terminates processes. This differs from the old code, which called kill unconditionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join breaks early on deadline and skips terminating remaining processes

In join(), the loop over processes uses `break` once the deadline has passed. Every process not yet visited is then never terminated. Those processes are daemon processes and keep running, flushing Redis and producing to Kafka after shutdown or across rebalances. With many shards, they can pile up as orphaned flushers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Default flusher_processes=1 contradicts per-shard intent

The CLI default of 1 is always passed to the factory, so the `max_processes or len(shards)` fallback (one process per shard) is never reached in production. The PR description says the flusher spawns a process per shard, and the class docstring says it creates one process per shard. Both are wrong for the default configuration, which still runs a single flusher process.

Zero assigned shards causes modulo-by-zero / empty map

If a consumer is assigned no partitions, `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty. `max_processes` then falls back to 0 and `num_processes` is 0. No flusher runs, and the loop is empty, so the modulo-by-zero is never hit. However, passing `--flusher-processes 0` while shards are assigned makes `num_processes` 0 and raises ZeroDivisionError in `i % self.num_processes`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from background thread

`_commit_loop` calls `commit_function` from a separate daemon thread. That function wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback, which is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer's poll/submit thread. Calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor run loop can race with stage/commit logic or the rebalance path. Commits should instead be gathered and issued from `poll()`.

Offsets skipped by compaction or transaction markers block commits forever

`get_committable_offsets` requires every integer between the last committed offset and the target to have been seen. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous; transactional control records and compaction both create gaps. When a gap occurs, commits stall permanently for that partition. The tracker also never removes state for revoked partitions.

Race between snapshot and mark_committed; dict iteration unsynchronized

`all_offsets.keys()` is iterated in the commit thread while the consumer thread may be inserting into the defaultdict at the same time. Separately, the per-partition lock creation done with `get` followed by `setdefault` is racy.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure

The queues are created with `queue.Queue()` and no maxsize, and `submit` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The docstring claims 'natural backpressure', but in practice a slow consumer will buffer unbounded messages in memory, which can lead to OOM.

close/join shut down the shared queue pool, breaking strategy after rebalance

On rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy. This shuts down `self.queue_pool`, which belongs to the factory and is shared across strategies. The next `create_with_partitions` call then reuses a pool whose queues are shut down and whose workers have exited, so every `put` raises `ShutDown`. The failure is swallowed by `submit`'s except block, which also marks the offset complete, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. In addition, `join` does not wait for the in-flight work to drain before the final commit, so processed offsets are lost and get reprocessed.

hash() on str is randomized per process

Python's `hash()` on strings is salted per process, so queue assignment is not stable across processes or restarts. This contradicts the docstring's claim of 'consistent hashing'. It is harmless within a single process, but the documentation is misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every cached deny now triggers a DB query, cache hits double-counted

When cached permissions deny a request, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which now always queries the DB. The singleflight cache-check was removed from it. So every first-time denied check hits the database. When the denial cache returns, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with the label "true". On the fallthrough path, the "false" label is incremented even when the cache was actually hit. Both make the cache metrics misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial test does not prove the cache bypass

This test is meant to show that the denial cache short-circuits the permission check. However, it sets the permission cache to map{dash1: false}, which would deny the request anyway. The test therefore passes whether or not the denial cache works. It should set dash1 to true so that only the denial cache can explain the deny.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial key uses raw subject UID and ambiguous concatenation

The denial key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw subject string, which can be a numeric ID or a UID. The permission cache instead uses the resolved userIdentifiers.UID, so the two caches key the same user differently. The key also omits the identity type, so a user and an anonymous or service-account identity with the same ID would share denial entries. Finally, name and parent are joined with '_', which also appears in names, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. Any of these collisions can deny the wrong subject or resource.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache defeats the newly-created-resource fix and blocks grants for 30s

When a check is denied, Check writes a denial entry for (user, action, name, folder) with a 30s TTL, and every later Check returns deny from that entry before looking at permissions. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions change. A user who checks a resource just before its permission row is visible (for example, a creator racing dashboard creation), or before being granted access, stays denied for up to 30s. This brings back the exact problem the PR is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in list

When `GrafanaRuleLoader` was replaced with `GrafanaRuleListItem`, the `key={key}` prop was dropped. This element is rendered inside `rules.map(...)`. Without a key, React warns and reconciles items by index. Since the list grows incrementally as pages load, items can be mismatched and lose state such as an open menu or modal.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item does nothing without ruler rule

The silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` is undefined, yet `canSilence` can be true via the prom abilities, so the 'Silence notifications' item is shown. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but nothing renders, so the action is a no-op for the user.

false_positives.candidate:
Export ability excludes Grafana recording rules

For prom rules, ModifyExport is supported only when `isAlertingRule` is true. The ruler-based version uses `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which also covers recording rules. As a result, Grafana recording rules lose the Export option in the list view.

Pause and Delete never shown in list view despite prom-based abilities

`canPause` and `canDelete` now include the prom-rule abilities, but the menu items still require a `rulerRule`. Pause is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and Delete on `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes a ruler rule, so users with permission silently lose the Pause and Delete actions there. The new test asserts exactly 4 items, which locks in this regression.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Queries are interpolated twice in the sharding path

runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on each target and then passes the subrequests to runSplitQuery, which calls applyTemplateVariables again on every subrequest. The test confirms this: the call count goes from 1 to 5. Running interpolation a second time on already-interpolated expressions can double-apply ad-hoc filters (request.filters) or re-escape values. It also adds per-shard overhead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID no longer included in plugin request log

The explicit `traceID` log param was removed. The replacement, `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, adds only contextual attributes such as endpoint, pluginId and dsName. Whether it also adds traceID depends on the infra logger's context providers, and the plugin log wrapper's FromContext falls back to `d.New()` when the type assertion fails, which drops all context. In that fallback case, "Plugin Request Completed" logs lose the traceID and all plugin and request details.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logged calls cannot be asserted

`FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, instead of `f`. Since LoggerMiddleware now always logs through `FromContext(ctx)`, tests that use TestLogger will never see the recorded Info calls. Returning `f` would keep those calls observable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding a method to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementations

`FromContext` is added to the public `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Any other implementations, such as fakes in other packages, test loggers or enterprise code, will stop compiling until they implement the new method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert race allows exceeding device limit

The limit check counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices across goroutines or instances can all see count < limit and all insert. The configured limit can therefore be exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RowsAffected==0 misreported as limit reached on MySQL

By default, MySQL reports only changed rows in RowsAffected. When an existing device updates with identical client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at (second precision), 0 rows are reported as affected. ErrDeviceLimitReached is then returned for a device that is already registered, and authentication is denied.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache set before store write lets rejected devices bypass the limit

tagDeviceUI writes the device to localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry stays in place. For the next 29 minutes, requests from that device hit the cache and return nil. Authentication then succeeds, so the device limit is only enforced on the first request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous request path

TagDevice used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout. It now runs synchronously on every anonymous authentication. When a device limit is set, each uncached request does a COUNT query and then an INSERT or UPDATE against the DB. This adds DB latency to every anonymous request. A slow or failing DB now delays or degrades anonymous auth, even when no limit is configured.

Raw error returned on limit with no proper authn error/status

When the limit is reached, Authenticate returns a plain error instead of a typed authn/errutil error. The client gets a generic failure with no clear HTTP status or message explaining that the anonymous device limit was reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists

Each batch of the cleanup loops logs at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the entire `ids` slice. These logs fire on every run even when nothing goes wrong. With large batch sizes (e.g. 32767), they write enormous error log lines, flood logs and alerting, and add overhead. They look like leftover debugging and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The interval for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and the PR description does not mention or justify it. Each job still has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap or queue back to back. That means 10x more DB load for snapshots, dashboard versions, query history and the rest. This looks like a leftover debugging change.

false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can delete the wrong rows when inserts run concurrently

The IDs are fetched with ORDER BY id DESC plus an OFFSET of MaxCount, then deleted in a separate statement outside any transaction. This already happens every batch. Concurrent inserts shift the offset between batches, so the result is no longer one consistent cut. The comment only claims under-deletion, but this offset behaviour should be considered and documented.

Quadratic string building for SQLite IN list

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` rebuilds the whole string on every iteration. That is O(n^2) for batches of tens of thousands of IDs. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

SQLite inline path keyed on configured batch size instead of actual ID count

The check for whether to inline IDs or use placeholders looks at the configured batch size, not at how many IDs this batch actually has. The placeholder path is still correct as long as len(ids) never exceeds the batch size. Checking len(ids) instead would make the limit handling more robust.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts base logger in context, dropping fields

Delete calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the base logger instead of `log`. The name, kind and method values built on the line above are therefore lost for downstream logging.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage metric

The asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded with recordStorageDuration rather than recordLegacyDuration. This skews storage metrics and hides legacy failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete metric uses name instead of kind label

On success, Delete calls recordStorageDuration with `name` in the kind position. This produces a metric label per object name, which is a cardinality explosion, and the label value is wrong.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy write derives from request context which is canceled after response

The goroutine wraps the request ctx with a timeout. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which is immediately after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls will therefore often fail with context canceled, and legacy storage silently diverges. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before applying the timeout. The same pattern appears at lines 110, 135 and 163.

Async legacy write errors are never logged

Errors from the background legacy writes are only counted in metrics, never logged. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Divergence between the stores is now invisible in logs.

Create error case mocks legacy, not storage; async calls unasserted

The case named "unified store fails" sets up the failure on the legacy mock via setupLegacyFn. The legacy and storage mocks share one mock instance, so the test passes by accident. None of the tests wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy calls.

Legacy update reuses objInfo concurrently/after request

objInfo is passed unchanged to the background legacy Update, while the old updateWrapper with the storage-updated object is no longer used. Patch-based objInfo is evaluated against the legacy object, so the legacy store may end up with different content than unified storage. The same objInfo is also used across goroutines after the request has finished.

Storage failure recorded as legacy duration metric

In Create, a failure from d.Storage.Create is recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Update has the same mistake at line 129. As a result, storage errors are attributed to the legacy store in metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check after acquiring write lock; concurrent callers all reload the manifest

After the read-locked check misses, the code takes the write lock but does not check the cache again. Several goroutines that miss at the same time line up on the lock. Each one then re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json, or makes the CDN request, one after another. They also overwrite the cache each time. A double-checked pattern (re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` when not in Dev, after taking `Lock`) would avoid this redundant serialized I/O. In production this happens at startup, or after an earlier failure has left the cache nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error result overwrites a previously cached valid value with nil

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`. If a reload fails, the cache is set to nil and the error is returned. This happens in Dev mode on every call, or with a transient file or CDN error. Any good assets cached earlier are lost, and later callers get errors or trigger reloads. Only update the cache when `err == nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is misleading

enableSqlExpressions negates the feature flag check and then returns false in both branches, so the flag has no effect. Disabling the feature is intentional, but the code reads as if the flag gates it. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the inverted negation could re-enable the DuckDB path without noticing. Replace this with a plain `return false` and a comment explaining the security reason.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL parser/command tests now fail against the stub DB

TablesList now calls the stub DB, whose RunCommands always returns "not implemented". The other legacy SQL path, UnmarshalSQLCommand, calls NewSQLCommand and so fails the same way. Any existing tests that parse SQL table lists or execute SQL commands will fail. The PR does not update or skip those tests and adds no test asserting that SQL expressions are rejected.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message misleading for SQL expressions

Users receive "sqlExpressions is not implemented", even when the sqlExpressions feature flag is on. In reality the feature was implemented and then deliberately disabled for security reasons. A clearer message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would tell users that turning on the flag will not help.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent builds of the same key and file index collisions

The cache lock is now taken only for the final map write. Two callers that both miss in getOrCreateIndex (for example, watch events or searches arriving during startup) will build the same key at the same time. For file-based indexes, both call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or corrupt the index. One built index also overwrites the other, and IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics get double-counted. Add per-key singleflight or re-check the cache under the lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates cache map without lock

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without holding cacheMu. Other goroutines can write to the map concurrently via BuildIndex. A concurrent map read and write can make the Go runtime throw a fatal error.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in parallel init workers

Inside the group.Go closures, `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables captured from the enclosing scope and written by several goroutines at once. Now that BuildIndex no longer holds a global lock, builds really do run concurrently, so these writes race. The result can be a wrong indexed count and corrupted error state. Use goroutine-local variables (`_, _, err := ...`) and an atomic counter.

Integration test disabled for postgres

This PR skips the storage server integration test on postgres instead of fixing the failure. The new startup-init behaviour therefore goes untested on postgres.

Search init now runs before the watcher, so events between index build and watch start are lost

Init now builds every index synchronously in the constructor. WatchWriteEvents is subscribed only after the indexes are built and starts from the latest RV at that moment. Any writes made while the indexes were being built are therefore never applied to the index. Init also now blocks NewResourceServer startup for the whole index build, with no timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias"

Each cleanup is registered with `get("alias")::remove` instead of the actual alias created in the loop. As a result, the created IDPs are never removed, and test state leaks into other tests. The same mistake appears at line 425.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache keeps stale IDP data after updates that leave login availability unchanged

In `update()`, `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` skips invalidating the login caches when an IDP stays login-eligible with the same organization. The cached query stores only internal IDs, and those are re-resolved through `getById`, so changed attributes like the display name are picked up. Ordering and membership stay correct too.

The gap is the `getById` path: `update()` calls `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which can return an org-aware wrapped model. The predicate is tested against that wrapper, whose `isEnabled()` also depends on the organization being enabled. So the decision to skip invalidation is based on org state, not only on the IDP's own fields.

The cached list is also not invalidated when an organization is disabled or enabled. That is why the bean has to re-check `isEnabled()`. However, the `onlyRealmBrokers` path in `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` (line 58) does not re-check it.

Login cache not invalidated when organization is removed or IDP is unlinked via org provider

The `ORG_ONLY` and `ALL` login caches are keyed only by realm and fetch mode. Invalidation happens only from this provider's `create`, `update` and `remove`.

Removing an organization or deleting its IDPs through other paths, such as `removeAll` on realm deletion, never registers a login-cache invalidation. The `getById` null check only catches IDPs that have been deleted outright.

When an organization is removed but its IDPs remain, possibly unlinked, the cached `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` results can still include IDPs that are no longer org-linked. The `REALM_ONLY` results can also miss IDPs that should now appear there.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns an arbitrary keystore provider

This method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (for example SUN or SunJSSE), not a BouncyCastle provider. Code that calls `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` or uses this provider for cipher or signature operations may get an unexpected provider or fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException`.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite length returns -1 and causes NegativeArraySizeException

`readLength` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). `readInteger` then calls `read(-1)`, which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of an `IOException`. In `readSequence` the loop is skipped and an empty list is returned. Malformed signatures therefore produce unchecked exceptions rather than a clean verification failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method with no default. Any existing external implementation of `CryptoProvider` will fail to compile, and at runtime an `AbstractMethodError` is thrown when `detectProvider` calls `order()` during sorting. Making it a `default` method (for example returning 0) would keep backward compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal listener gated on V1 feature only

The listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`, which skips cleanup when only V2 is enabled. That avoids the UnsupportedOperationException from `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled`. However, if V1 and V2 are both enabled, `management()` returns MgmtPermissionsV2, so deleting a client calls `setPermissionsEnabled` and throws. Separately, V2 per-client resources and permissions are never removed when their client is deleted, leaving orphaned resources.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission only finds resources whose type is 'Clients'

Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)`, and no type is ever set on them. Only the 'Clients' all-resource has type 'Clients'. `findByType` therefore returns at most that all-resource, so the method returns {"Clients"} instead of client IDs. As a result, listing clients will not work through per-client permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when all-clients resource missing

`getResourceTypeResource` can return null, for example when a realm's admin-permissions client was initialized before 'Clients' was added to the schema. The null is passed to `findByResource` and then dereferenced in `resource.getScopes()`, which throws an NPE. That would surface as a 500 on admin client endpoints.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Per-client permission shadows all-clients permission

If a per-client resource exists, only that resource is evaluated and the 'Clients' all-resource is never checked. For example, a per-client VIEW permission removes a MANAGE grant the admin has through an all-clients permission, because the fallback only runs when no specific resource exists. Note that the caller's `canManage` short-circuit does not cover this case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled test does not check exit code or the check subcommand

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message for the metadata subcommand. It does not verify the new exit code 4.

It also does not cover the check subcommand. That leaves the new FEATURE_DISABLED contract untested.

Recreate exit code changed from 4 to 3, and 4 now means feature disabled

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was 4 and is now 3. Code 4 is reused for FEATURE_DISABLED.

Existing scripts, and the operator if it consumes this code, that treat exit code 4 as "recreate needed" will now get a different meaning for the same value. A disabled feature would be interpreted as a recreate decision, and real recreate results (3) would be treated as unknown errors.

Any consumer in the operator should be checked and updated together with this change.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage on VIEW permission

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE). An admin who holds only the 'view' scope on all groups is therefore treated as able to manage groups, for example creating top-level groups via addTopLevelGroup. This is a privilege escalation. The check should require only the MANAGE scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs, not group IDs

In V2, group resources are named by the group ID, but the code passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission (which looks the resource up by name) and adds groupResource.getId() to the result set. The returned set therefore holds authz resource IDs instead of group IDs. The users search and count group filters will match nothing, or fall back to the all-groups resource. Use groupResource.getName() in both places.

false_positives.candidate:
Group permission scan now runs on every user search

searchForUser now always calls getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. That method calls users().canView(), which can itself trigger a policy evaluation, and it then evaluates permissions for every group resource. Previously this work was skipped when users().canView() was already true. The cost is duplicated or extra evaluation on every user search.

Permission results not filtered by resource ID

Unlike UserPermissionsV2, this loop accepts a matching scope from any permission returned by the evaluation, without checking permission.getResourceId() against the evaluated resource. Scopes granted on other resources could therefore satisfy the check for this group. Filter the permissions by resource ID, as UserPermissionsV2 does.

Possible NPE when all-groups resource is missing

getResourceTypeResource can return null, for example when the schema is unsupported or the 'Groups' resource is absent. hasPermission then passes that null to policyStore.findByResource and later calls resource.getScopes(), which throws a NullPointerException. A null check is needed before using the resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Italian text placed into Lithuanian translation

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian bundle was replaced with Italian text ('Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:'). Lithuanian users will see Italian. The same mistake was made for loginTotpStep1 in login/messages_lt.properties.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Traditional Chinese text in Simplified Chinese bundle

The new totpStep1 value ('在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一') is Traditional Chinese, but this is the zh_CN (Simplified Chinese) bundle. It should use Simplified characters, e.g. 在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一.

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor check skips leftover English anchors and is order-sensitive

The loop advances the English matcher once per translated anchor and compares the tags pairwise. However, replaceFirst removes the first occurrence of that tag anywhere in the value, not necessarily the one just matched, so for repeated tags it may strip the wrong instance. Also, href attributes are compared verbatim, which is acceptable, but the anchors removed here are never passed through the sanitizer at all, so attribute content is never validated beyond the equality check.

English file path derivation is fragile

The path to the English file is built with replaceAll on the whole absolute path. The 'resources-community' replacement and the '_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties' pattern operate on the full string; for example, '_en.properties' itself maps to itself. Any directory component containing these patterns would be altered. If the English file does not exist, a RuntimeException is thrown instead of a reported message, which aborts verification of the file.

Java MessageFormat syntax used in i18next-based account UI

The account UI uses i18next interpolation with double braces ({{0}}), as the other keys in this file do. Changing error-invalid-multivalued-size to single-brace Java ChoiceFormat syntax ({0}, {2,choice,...}) means the React UI will not substitute the values. Users will see the raw '{0} ... {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}' text. The same problem applies to the admin-ui messages_en.properties change.

Raw plaintext recovery codes sent to user storage

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from background thread

`_commit_loop` calls `commit_function` from a separate daemon thread. That function wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback, which is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer's poll/submit thread. Calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor run loop can race with stage/commit logic or the rebalance path. Commits should instead be gathered and issued from `poll()`.

close/join shut down the shared queue pool, breaking strategy after rebalance

On rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy. This shuts down `self.queue_pool`, which belongs to the factory and is shared across strategies. The next `create_with_partitions` call then reuses a pool whose queues are shut down and whose workers have exited, so every `put` raises `ShutDown`. The failure is swallowed by `submit`'s except block, which also marks the offset complete, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. In addition, `join` does not wait for the in-flight work to drain before the final commit, so processed offsets are lost and get reprocessed.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure

The queues are created with `queue.Queue()` and no maxsize, and `submit` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The docstring claims 'natural backpressure', but in practice a slow consumer will buffer unbounded messages in memory, which can lead to OOM.

Offsets skipped by compaction or transaction markers block commits forever

`get_committable_offsets` requires every integer between the last committed offset and the target to have been seen. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous; transactional control records and compaction both create gaps. When a gap occurs, commits stall permanently for that partition. The tracker also never removes state for revoked partitions.

Race between snapshot and mark_committed; dict iteration unsynchronized

`all_offsets.keys()` is iterated in the commit thread while the consumer thread may be inserting into the defaultdict at the same time. Separately, the per-partition lock creation done with `get` followed by `setdefault` is racy.

hash() on str is randomized per process

Python's `hash()` on strings is salted per process, so queue assignment is not stable across processes or restarts. This contradicts the docstring's claim of 'consistent hashing'. It is harmless within a single process, but the documentation is misleading.

When only the first zunionstore runs, `span_count` is taken from it, which is fine. The eviction step uses `zpopmin`, which removes the spans with the lowest scores (the earliest end timestamps). This can evict the root/segment span, so the flushed segment loses its root and `is_segment` detection breaks. Separately, the hardcoded 1000 limit ignores the configurable `max_segment_spans`.

__reduce__ passes redis_ttl as segment_page_size

`__reduce__` passes its arguments positionally, so the 4th argument (`redis_ttl`) lands in the `segment_page_size` parameter. In the multiprocessing path, which pickles the buffer, worker processes therefore get a page size of 3600 and the default TTL. This bug predates the PR but becomes more relevant now that the PR changes the buffer constructor's parameters.

The PR adds span-count eviction in Lua and removes the `max_segment_spans` check in Python. No test covers a segment that exceeds 1000 spans, so it is unverified which spans are evicted or that the root span is preserved.

The bigger problem is the invalidation design: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` must be called with exactly the same project set that was queried. Nothing in this PR calls it when the allowlist option changes. As a result, allowlist changes take up to 60s to apply for every project combination, which contradicts the 'always latest configuration' note at line 50. The tests that patch `options` can also be affected by stale cache entries left from earlier tests.

Negated queries (e.g. `!event.type:error`, which selects transactions) would get the `sum(sample_weight)` transform. That produces wrong counts, or a query failure on the transactions storage.

`sum(sample_weight)` assumes every event has `sample_weight`. Events ingested before the feature, or without a client sample rate, will have null weight and be dropped from the count. Using something like `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)` would avoid undercounting errors.

A `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit was added to the repository. This looks accidental and will break clones and CI that try to resolve the submodule.

`project_id in allowlist` scans the list once for each project, which is O(n*m). Converting the allowlist to a set first would make each lookup constant time.

Fallback locales are never loaded outside controller requests

Fallbacks module is included into whatever backend class is current

`I18n.backend.class.send(:include, ...)` depends on which backend is active when the initializer runs. The pluralization line above targets `Simple` explicitly. If a plugin or a later initializer swaps the backend, fallbacks silently stop applying.

No tests for the new fallback behaviour

The PR adds no specs covering the fallback order (user locale, then site locale, then English) or the loading of fallback locales.

sendAddGuestsEmails is passed `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`. If a submitted email was already an attendee, that existing attendee receives a fresh 'scheduled' email instead of the 'guests added' notification. Pass uniqueGuests.

The candidate's uniqueGuests fix addresses that underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

EventManager is built from ctx.user and ctx.user's credentials. When an attendee or a team admin adds guests, updateCalendarAttendees runs with credentials that do not own the booking's calendar references. The update fails or throws, and because it is not caught, the request errors even though the attendee rows are already saved. Use the booking user's credentials (booking.user.credentials) instead.

No restriction on cancelled or past bookings, and no limit on number of guests

The handler does not check booking status. Any attendee can add an unbounded list of guests to any booking they belong to, including cancelled ones. Each added guest triggers outbound email, so this can be abused to spam arbitrary addresses.

Error message fallback never applies

The message is built with a template string that always produces a non-empty value, even when err.data is missing (e.g. 'undefined: ...'). As a result, the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never be used.

Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic

The code reads the backup codes, checks them in memory, and then writes the re-encrypted list back with no transaction or compare-and-set. Concurrent login requests can all validate the same code before any of them writes, so a single-use code can be used several times. A concurrent write can also overwrite another request's update.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: backup codes are checked and consumed in memory before a non-atomic write, allowing concurrent login requests to reuse the same supposedly one-time code.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`handleSetup` calls `formatBackupCode`, which is declared later with `const`. This works only because the call happens at runtime, after render. The blob object URL is also never revoked when the modal closes, so it leaks for the life of the page.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate emphasizes a different concern in its title, it explicitly identifies the unreleased blob object URL when the modal closes and the resulting memory leak, matching the golden comment's missing cleanup on component unmount.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code path skips password check for external-TOTP flow

The password check runs only when `!credentials.totpCode`, but the backup-code branch is selected by `credentials.backupCode`. A client can send a valid backup code together with any non-empty `totpCode`, which skips the password verification. Because the backupCode branch is taken first, the totpCode is never validated. A backup code alone then grants login without the password, making it a single factor.

Unvalidated backupCode type crashes handler

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` assumes the value is a string. A non-string value, such as a number or an array, throws and returns a 500. The client also always sends `backupCode` (possibly an empty string) alongside `code`, and the request is routed only by truthiness. Nothing validates the format or type of the value.

Lost-access option unavailable in external TOTP flow

When `totpEmail` is set (Google/SAML users with 2FA), the page shows ExternalTotpFooter, which has no 'Lost access' button. Those users cannot use their backup codes. This is also the only flow where the password check is legitimately skipped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

In that case `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` does nothing. Collective hosts' calendars are silently ignored, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to fix.

Reschedule merge only deletes the first host's old calendar event
