Recurring cancel repeats the full delete for every reference and ignores other hosts' credentials

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

All app modules are still imported eagerly at module load

It also adds a risk: if any app module throws during load, its promise rejects with no handler attached. That surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection at startup.

The entries should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call sites should invoke them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

forEach(async) in requestReschedule leaves deletions unawaited

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside each callback. The returned promises are discarded, so the calendar and video deletions are fire-and-forget.

Any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The mutation may also return before the events are actually deleted.

Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` that reads `.calendar` directly will get a Promise. Because a Promise is always truthy, those callers will either break or wrongly treat a missing calendar as present.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Inconsistent metric tag key 'shards' vs 'shard'

The `wait_produce` timer uses the tag key `shards`, while the neighbouring metrics use `shard`. This inconsistency breaks dashboards and queries that group by the shard tag.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the flush metrics inconsistently tag the shard identifier as 'shards' in wait_produce versus 'shard' in neighboring metrics, preventing consistent aggregation and dashboard/query grouping.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process misses SpawnProcess

The processes are created through `get_context('spawn').Process`, so they are `SpawnProcess` instances. That class derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process`. The checks `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` are therefore always False. As a result, hung processes are never killed before a replacement is spawned, and join never terminates processes. This differs from the old code, which called kill unconditionally.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: processes created via get_context('spawn').Process are SpawnProcess instances not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance check is always false and hung processes are not killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join breaks early on deadline and skips terminating remaining processes

In join(), the loop over processes uses `break` once the deadline has passed. Every process not yet visited is then never terminated. Those processes are daemon processes and keep running, flushing Redis and producing to Kafka after shutdown or across rebalances. With many shards, they can pile up as orphaned flushers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: an early break when the deadline elapses skips termination of remaining flusher processes, leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Zero assigned shards causes modulo-by-zero / empty map

If a consumer is assigned no partitions, `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty. `max_processes` then falls back to 0 and `num_processes` is 0. No flusher runs, and the loop is empty, so the modulo-by-zero is never hit. However, passing `--flusher-processes 0` while shards are assigned makes `num_processes` 0 and raises ZeroDivisionError in `i % self.num_processes`.

Default flusher_processes=1 contradicts per-shard intent

The CLI default of 1 is always passed to the factory, so the `max_processes or len(shards)` fallback (one process per shard) is never reached in production. The PR description says the flusher spawns a process per shard, and the class docstring says it creates one process per shard. Both are wrong for the default configuration, which still runs a single flusher process.

An admin who holds only the 'view' scope on all groups is therefore treated as able to manage groups, for example creating top-level groups via addTopLevelGroup. This is a privilege escalation. In V2, group resources are named by the group ID, but the code passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission (which looks the resource up by name) and adds groupResource.getId() to the result set. The returned set therefore holds authz resource IDs instead of group IDs. The users search and count group filters will match nothing, or fall back to the all-groups resource. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: groupResource.getId() is passed to hasPermission and added to the result, but the resource is named by the group ID and callers expect group IDs. The candidate's recommendation to use getName() matches the golden concern about aligning with resource names and the interface contract.

Permission results not filtered by resource ID

Unlike UserPermissionsV2, this loop accepts a matching scope from any permission returned by the evaluation, without checking permission.getResourceId() against the evaluated resource. That method calls users().canView(), which can itself trigger a policy evaluation, and it then evaluates permissions for every group resource. Previously this work was skipped when users().canView() was already true. The cost is duplicated or extra evaluation on every user search.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

Although it also raises unrelated SPI/constructor breakage and frames the mismatch as a parsing failure, it identifies the same underlying documentation issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Token issuance fails for grant types without a registered factory

`encodeTokenId` throws IllegalStateException when the grant type stored in the client session context has no known shortcut. That attribute is set from the raw `grant_type` form parameter. Any flow that sets an unrecognized grant type will now fail access-token creation with a 500 error. Examples are custom grants whose factory id differs from the grant_type value, or the legacy token exchange path. Consider falling back to UNKNOWN instead of throwing.

Duplicate-shortcut detection ineffective

If two grants share a shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts` loses an entry while `grantsToShortcuts` keeps both, so the sizes differ and an error is thrown. However, the lazy refresh methods can later overwrite mappings without any validation. Duplicates introduced by grants deployed at runtime are therefore not detected, and decoding becomes ambiguous.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw plaintext recovery codes sent to user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the generatedCodes list as JSON and passes it to user.credentialManager().updateCredential, which hands it to every federated user storage provider supporting the type. These are the raw recovery codes, not hashed. External storages will therefore receive and likely persist plaintext recovery codes. `all_offsets.keys()` is iterated in the commit thread while the consumer thread may be inserting into the defaultdict at the same time. Separately, the per-partition lock creation done with `get` followed by `setdefault` is racy.

The unscheduled query does not filter out cancelled=true, so cancelled reminders can be scheduled and sent. The cancellation query also lacks a method: EMAIL filter.

One SendGrid failure aborts the entire cancellation batch

The whole cancellation loop sits inside a single try block. If any client.request call throws, for example because of a null referenceId or a rate limit, the loop stops. The remaining cancellations are skipped and the deletes already queued are never awaited. Error handling should happen per reminder.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive

The blacklist entries are lowercased, but guest emails are compared as typed. Duplicate detection against existing attendees is also an exact-case comparison. A mixed-case variant of a blacklisted or existing email therefore bypasses both checks and gets added. Lowercase the guest emails before comparing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same blacklist bypass: blacklist entries are lowercased while guest emails are compared without normalization, so mixed-case variants evade the check. The extra duplicate-check note does not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed as isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner. A team admin who is not the owner, or an owner who is not reported as an admin, fails the check. Unless they are also the organizer or an attendee, they get FORBIDDEN, even though the variable name says either role should be enough. Use || instead of &&.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same permission bug: the team admin/owner check incorrectly uses &&, requiring both roles, when it should use || so either role grants permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

Scheduled emails sent to all input guests rather than only newly added ones

sendAddGuestsEmails is passed `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`. If a submitted email was already an attendee, that existing attendee receives a fresh 'scheduled' email instead of the 'guests added' notification. Pass uniqueGuests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in sendAddGuestsEmails: using the full input guests list causes existing attendees to receive a scheduled email instead of the guests-added notification. The candidate's uniqueGuests fix targets that same recipient-selection issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

EventManager is built from ctx.user and ctx.user's credentials. When an attendee or a team admin adds guests, updateCalendarAttendees runs with credentials that do not own the booking's calendar references. The update fails or throws, and because it is not caught, the request errors even though the attendee rows are already saved. Use the booking user's credentials (booking.user.credentials) instead.

No restriction on cancelled or past bookings, and no limit on number of guests

The handler does not check booking status. Any attendee can add an unbounded list of guests to any booking they belong to, including cancelled ones. Each added guest triggers outbound email, so this can be abused to spam arbitrary addresses.

Error message fallback never applies

The message is built with a template string that always produces a non-empty value, even when err.data is missing (e.g. 'undefined: ...'). As a result, the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never be used.

Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic

The code reads the backup codes, checks them in memory, and then writes the re-encrypted list back with no transaction or compare-and-set. Concurrent login requests can all validate the same code before any of them writes, so a single-use code can be used several times. A concurrent write can also overwrite another request's update.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same race condition: backup codes are checked and mutated in memory before being written back without atomicity, so concurrent requests can validate the same one-time code multiple times.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
formatBackupCode used before its const declaration

`handleSetup` calls `formatBackupCode`, which is declared later with `const`. This works only because the call happens at runtime, after render. The blob object URL is also never revoked when the modal closes, so it leaks for the life of the page.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the backup-code blob object URL is never revoked when the modal closes, causing a leak. This is the same underlying memory-leak issue as the golden comment, despite also mentioning a separate declaration-order concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code path skips password check for external-TOTP flow

The password check runs only when `!credentials.totpCode`, but the backup-code branch is selected by `credentials.backupCode`. A client can send a valid backup code together with any non-empty `totpCode`, which skips the password verification. Because the backupCode branch is taken first, the totpCode is never validated. A backup code alone then grants login without the password, making it a single factor.

Unvalidated backupCode type crashes handler

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` assumes the value is a string. A non-string value, such as a number or an array, throws and returns a 500. The client also always sends `backupCode` (possibly an empty string) alongside `code`, and the request is routed only by truthiness. Nothing validates the format or type of the value.

Lost-access option unavailable in external TOTP flow

When `totpEmail` is set (Google/SAML users with 2FA), the page shows ExternalTotpFooter, which has no 'Lost access' button. Those users cannot use their backup codes. This is also the only flow where the password check is legitimately skipped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.

Crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` gives undefined when the array is empty or null, and the next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. This throws a TypeError for any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar. Previously the code used `?.`. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same null/empty destinationCalendar destructuring bug: mainHostDestinationCalendar becomes undefined and .integration is accessed without optional chaining, causing a TypeError. The candidate describes the exact code and fix even without naming the methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

Fallback lookup can never match

The `find` that compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it can never match anything. The previous fallback to the destination calendar's externalId is lost. Update and delete then go to undefined in update, or to `primary` in delete, instead of the configured calendar. The same issue appears in deleteEvent at line 317.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same broken calendar fallback lookup: the comparison of cal.externalId to externalCalendarId cannot succeed, so update/delete operations target the wrong calendar instead of the configured one.

false_positives.candidate:
Team member calendars dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. In that case `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` does nothing. Collective hosts' calendars are silently ignored, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to fix.

When `newBookingId` is set, only the first `_calendar` reference (`find`) is deleted. With multiple hosts there are several references, so the other hosts keep stale events on their calendars after a reschedule.

Recurring cancel repeats the full delete for every reference and ignores other hosts' credentials

Inside the per-reference loop, the recurring branch iterates over all of the organizer's calendar credentials and all updated bookings. It does this once for each reference, so the same deletes run multiple times. It also only uses the first `_calendar` ref and the organizer's credentials, so other hosts' recurring events are never deleted.

Inverted slug condition for org creation

The original code set `slug` when billing was disabled (`!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`). The new code sets it when billing is enabled, which bypasses the paid slug request flow. When billing is disabled, organizations are now created without a slug. This change is unrelated to the PR and is a regression.

BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. The payload is now an array or null, depending on the code path. BOOKING_REJECTED was changed to `[]`, so these expectations should be checked for consistency.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach pushes to apiDeletes after it is awaited

The recurring-cancel branch uses `forEach(async ...)` and awaits `getCalendar` before pushing into `apiDeletes`. Those pushes happen after the synchronous code has moved on, so `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` has already captured the array and misses them.

As a result, calendar deletions for recurring bookings are not awaited, and their errors become unhandled rejections. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: async callbacks inside forEach are not awaited, so calendar deletion promises are missed and can reject unhandled. The candidate gives a specific recurring-cancel manifestation and recommends the same for...of/Promise.all fix.

false_positives.candidate:
All app modules are still imported eagerly at module load

Each property is written as `import("./x")`, and that call runs as soon as the object literal is evaluated. So every app package is still loaded when `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, and nothing is lazy. The PR's goal of deferring app loading is not met.

It also adds a risk: if any app module throws during load, its promise rejects with no handler attached. That surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection at startup.

The entries should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call sites should invoke them.

forEach(async) in requestReschedule leaves deletions unawaited

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside each callback. The returned promises are discarded, so the calendar and video deletions are fire-and-forget.

Any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The mutation may also return before the events are actually deleted.

getCalendarCredentials now returns calendar as a Promise

`calendar` in each returned item is now a `Promise<Calendar|null>`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it.

Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` that reads `.calendar` directly will get a Promise. Because a Promise is always truthy, those callers will either break or wrongly treat a missing calendar as present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
